Welcome to our October Newsletter! This month, we highlight how the Volkswagen Group is strengthening Europe’s future and competitiveness through transformation, innovation and close cooperation between business and policymakers. From the “For Europe” commitment and discussions around Europe’s competitiveness and “Made in Europe” to the Volkswagen Group’s latest delivery figures and nine-month result, October put key strategic and business topics in focus. The Electric Urban Car Family and Volkswagen Group Design also demonstrate how shared expertise and synergies can strengthen distinctive brand identities. 🔍 Explore the 7️⃣ highlights that shaped October: 🌍 1. For Europe: Commitment to Europe’s future and competitiveness With its “For Europe” commitment, the Volkswagen Group underscores its role as a driving force for Europe’s future and competitiveness. The Group is addressing competitive and transformative pressures with attractive products, future-oriented technologies and the largest transformation program in its history. 🔗 Read the full press release here: For Europe: Volkswagen Group is committed to Europe’s future and competitiveness 🎬 2. What Europe needs to succeed Europe has the industrial strength, technological expertise and innovative power to succeed. Volkswagen Group CEO Oliver Blume shares what Europe needs to sustainably strengthen its competitiveness and economic success. 🏭 3. “Made in Europe” in a growing geopolitical competition What does “Made in Europe” mean in a time of growing geopolitical competition? According to Thomas Steg, General Representative of Volkswagen Group & Head of Group Public Affairs, Europe should not underestimate its own strength. With more than 450 million inhabitants, the European single market remains attractive globally, while a level playing field and fair competition are becoming increasingly important. 🔗 Read the full interview here: Why the Volkswagen Group is advocating for Made in Europe 🎬 4. “For Europe”: Highlights from Paris At the “For Europe” event on the eve of the Mondial de l’Auto in Paris, the Volkswagen Group demonstrated how Europe’s industrial strength can be translated into competitive products, technologies and value creation. Welcome back! Anthropic shares are already trading, Google shipped a model nobody can use, and the agent race quietly became a fight over permissions. In today's Atlas Newsletter: Trade Anthropic shares before Anthropic has shares: A crypto exchange opened pre-IPO trading days after the S-1 landed, with a 500,000 USDT prize pool attached. Google built its best cybersecurity model and will not let you use it: Gemini 4 Carbon finds vulnerabilities at 88.2% and writes exploits at 54.8%, and the access list is the product. The AI race moved to who writes the permission slip: One standard governs what an agent may do to an IT record, another governs what it may do to a microscope. Google spent $51 billion in one quarter and the market took $500 billion back: Cloud revenue doubled, free cash flow went negative, and Alphabet had its worst day in 20 years. PS: Want to collaborate with the biggest GTM engine and distribution moat for AI companies? You can feature your tool with us and reach millions. Trade Anthropic shares before Anthropic has shares Anthropic filed its S-1 this week, setting up what could be the largest IPO in history.  Within days, crypto exchange BingX opened pre-IPO trading on it and attached a 500,000 USDT prize pool, with eligible new users claiming $15 worth of ANTHROPIC for placing a trade. BingX runs this through its TradFi suite, which already carries stocks, indices, forex and commodities alongside perpetual futures and copy trading.  The platform reports more than 40 million users. Chief Strategy Officer Kevin Lee framed the launch around giving users “timely insights, broader market access, and deeper context.” What is being traded is exposure to a valuation, on a crypto exchange, for a company whose shares do not yet exist publicly.  Pricing comes from the platform rather than a regulated secondary market, which means the usual reference points for whether a quote is fair are unavailable. The filing itself is worth reading separately. Anthropic put pharmaceutical work near the front of its case, saying Claude already helps drug companies with discovery and has cut clinical trial report writing “from months to minutes.”  The same document warns that losing control of sufficiently powerful AI systems could become “a global security threat of the first order,” and elsewhere notes its own drug programs may never generate revenue.
